captions.text: One night of sleep. One EEG channel. One stage label for every 30 seconds.
This film walks through the math behind every step, then what the evidence does and does not show.
EEG measures a voltage difference between two electrodes on the scalp. It does not read thoughts.
Our channel is Fpz minus Cz, recorded in microvolts. One point on the trace is one voltage reading.
A computer cannot store a continuous curve. It keeps samples at regular moments.
Our recording uses 100 samples per second, so one value every 0.01 seconds.
Sampling sets a ceiling: the Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate, here 50 Hz.
A 70 Hz wave sampled at 100 Hz lands on the same points as a 30 Hz wave. That is aliasing.
We cut the night into 30-second epochs. At 100 Hz, each epoch holds 3,000 numbers.
So one epoch is a vector of 3,000 real numbers, paired with one reference stage label y.
Each epoch gets one of five labels, coded 0 to 4. The codes are names, not depth: REM = 4 is not deeper than N3 = 3.
Old sleep stages 3 and 4 are merged into N3. Movement and unknown epochs are left out of the five classes.
The evaluated cohort: 20 participants, 39 recorded nights and 42,307 retained epochs from Sleep-EDF Expanded.
Epochs from the same person are strongly related, so the data must be split by person, not by epoch.
In each fold, 16 people train the model, 2 people choose the checkpoint and 2 people are kept for testing.
Ten folds rotate the held-out people, so every participant is tested exactly once and never sits in two sets.
A sine wave has three knobs. Amplitude A sets its size.
Frequency f sets how many cycles happen each second.
Phase φ sets where in its cycle the wave starts.
Real signals are sums of waves. Here: a 2 Hz wave of size 20 plus a 12 Hz wave of size 5.
The recorded trace only shows the sum. The individual parts are hidden inside it.
For a sine wave over full cycles, the average of x² equals A²/2.
Double the amplitude and the power grows four times. Magnitude and power are different quantities.
The DFT compares the signal with a cosine and a sine at each test frequency.
Wrap the signal around a circle at that frequency. When the frequency matches, the wrapped curve leans to one side.
Measure that lean for every frequency and peaks appear at 2 Hz and 12 Hz.
Each DFT output is a complex number with a real part a and an imaginary part b.
We keep the magnitude |X| and drop the phase. The FFT is simply a fast way to compute the same DFT.
One FFT over all 30 seconds tells which frequencies exist, but not when they happen.
The STFT slides a 2-second Hamming window forward 1 second at a time and runs an FFT at each stop.
Stacking the 29 windows gives a time-frequency picture of one epoch.
Cutting a short piece of signal creates hard edges, and hard edges smear energy into nearby frequencies.
The Hamming window weights the middle and fades the edges. Leakage drops, at the cost of a slightly wider peak.
Count the windows: 29 time steps. Count the one-sided FFT bins: 129 frequencies. One epoch becomes a 129 × 29 grid.
Bins are 0.39 Hz apart, but zero-padding from 200 to 256 points adds bins, not new information.
Spectral magnitudes span huge ranges, so we take the natural logarithm. A 100× gap becomes about 4.6 units.
This is log-magnitude, not log-power. The tiny ε = 10⁻⁶ prevents ln(0) = −∞.
Colors are only for people. The network never sees colors.
It receives a 129 × 29 matrix of real numbers for every epoch.
Standardizing asks one question: how many standard deviations is this value from the mean?
12, with mean 10 and SD 2, becomes z = 1. The pattern of the data does not change, only its center and scale.
Our statistics are computed separately for each frequency bin, across every epoch and time step of a night.
That gives 129 means and 129 standard deviations. A floor of 10⁻³ stops division by a tiny SD.
Baseline: the statistics come only from the training participants, then the same numbers are used for every night.
R1: every night uses its own statistics, including validation and test nights. That makes R1 transductive.
Why might per-night statistics help? Suppose one night was recorded with a different gain a.
The STFT is linear, so the gain becomes a constant shift ln a in the log-magnitude features.
Per-night standardization cancels the shift. Ideal case only: real nights can differ in more complex ways.
There is a catch. A night's mean also depends on how much of each sleep stage the night contains.
A wake-heavy night and a deep-sleep-heavy night get different statistics even with perfect recording. Per-night normalization is a trade-off.
A training batch holds 32 sequences. Each sequence has 20 consecutive epochs, and each epoch is a 1 × 129 × 29 image.
Twenty epochs cover ten minutes. The CNN reads all 640 images at once, then they are regrouped into sequences for the GRU.
A single unit multiplies inputs by learned weights and adds a bias: 0.5·1 − 0.2·2 + 0.3 = 0.4.
Convolution slides the same 3 × 3 weights over the whole image, producing a feature map. In PyTorch this is technically cross-correlation.
ReLU keeps positive values and turns negatives into zero. Without it, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear map.
Max pooling keeps the largest value in each 2 × 2 block, halving height and width.
Three blocks of convolution, BatchNorm, ReLU and pooling shrink the image while adding feature channels.
Global average pooling turns 128 feature maps into one vector, then a linear layer gives the 128-number epoch embedding.
BatchNorm normalizes activations inside the CNN, per feature channel. It is a different step from our per-night input normalization.
Dropout with p = 0.3 switches off random activations during training only. model.eval() makes both layers fixed rules.
A GRU carries a hidden state h from one epoch to the next, mixing in each new epoch embedding e_t.
The reset gate r limits old context when proposing a candidate n. The update gate z decides how much old state to keep.
A bidirectional GRU runs twice: once forward in time and once backward. Two layers, 128 hidden units per direction.
Each epoch gets 128 + 128 = 256 context features. Context stops at the 20-epoch window; there is no memory of the whole night.
The classifier maps 256 features to five logits per epoch. Logits can be negative and need not sum to 1.
Softmax exponentiates and divides by the total. With logit ln 4 for N2 and 0 for the rest, N2 gets 4 / 8 = 0.5.
The prediction is the largest logit. A probability of 0.9 is not automatically right 90% of the time.
Training uses cross-entropy: minus the log of the probability the model gives to the true class.
Confident and correct costs little. Confident and wrong is punished hard: p = 0.01 costs 4.6.
N1 is rare and hard, so N1 mistakes are weighted 1.5 times. The loss is divided by the sum of the weights used.
A sequence does not get one answer: all 20 epochs keep their own label and add their own term to the loss.
The gradient of the loss for each logit is simple: p − 1 for the true class and p for every other class.
True class N1 with p = 0.2 gives −0.8, so its score should rise. N2 with p = 0.6 gives +0.6, so its score should fall.
AdamW keeps a running average of the gradient (m) and of its square (v), then scales each step parameter by parameter.
Learning rate 10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻⁴, and gradients clipped to a norm of 1 to avoid occasional violent steps.
Low training loss is not the goal. The goal is good predictions for people the model has never seen.
We keep the checkpoint with the best validation macro-F1, stopping after 10 epochs without improvement or at 60 epochs.
At inference, 20-epoch windows slide forward 5 epochs at a time, so most epochs are predicted by several windows.
We average the logits, not labels or probabilities. Softmax of an average is not the average of softmaxes.
Each scored epoch is counted by true stage (row) and predicted stage (column). These are R1 test counts.
The diagonal is correct: 34,266 of 42,307 epochs, a pooled accuracy of 80.99%.
Recall asks: of all true N1 epochs, how many did we catch? 1,253 of 2,804, or 44.7%.
Precision asks: of everything predicted N1, how much was right? 1,253 of 3,220, or 38.9%.
Their harmonic mean: pooled N1 F1 = 0.416. An accuracy near 81% hides this weak class.
Macro-F1 averages the five class F1 scores, so rare N1 counts as much as common N2.
Our headline goes one step further: compute macro-F1 for each person, then average the 20 people equally.
The baseline collapsed on particular test nights. One night was predicted entirely as a single class.
Four diagnostic rounds found no confirmed pairing, timing, channel or label-alignment defect.
Subject-mean macro-F1: baseline 56.42%, R1 74.86%, full-night sensitivity 71.84%. Pooled accuracy rose from 65.00% to 80.99%.
R1 changed normalization and retrained the weights together, and it was chosen after seeing the baseline failures. It is post-hoc.
The full-night sensitivity run takes statistics from the complete recording, without hypnogram-based trimming.
Training and scored epochs stay exactly the same. Only the range used for the statistics changes. It is still transductive.
A paired bootstrap redraws the 20 participants with replacement, 1,000 times, using the same draw for both runs.
Full-night minus R1: −3.02 points, 95% interval −7.12 to +1.22. It crosses zero: not enough evidence of a difference, and not proof they are equal.
Ten held-out folds tell a less tidy story. R1 improved pooled macro-F1 in all ten folds, but folds 0 and 9 stay comparatively weak.
Each fold pools only two test participants, and training sets overlap, so folds are not independent samples.
Per-class recall shows which stages are recovered. N1 is still the hardest: 44.7% with R1, 39.5% with full-night.
Better overall numbers do not solve every class.
Three small validation-only pilots tried to fix N1: logit adjustment, head-only retraining and a sequence decoder.
None reached the locked +1.00 point macro-F1 gate. All were rejected and the original settings were kept.
A provenance audit checked 78 participants: 30 had documented development exposure and 48 have unresolved history.
Zero are certified independent. Unresolved does not mean unused, so there is no clean external test yet.
Read every number within these limits: post-hoc selection, one model seed, and normalization that sees each test night.
The protocol differs from the original SST paper. This is neither a replication nor clinical validation, nor an online system.
Sampling, STFT, log, normalization, CNN, BiGRU, loss, AdamW, averaging, metrics, bootstrap: one connected system.
R1 scored higher in this cohort, and we know exactly which data, transforms and averaging produced it.
Next gate: a locked protocol on genuinely independent participants, after human approval.
